title: The march to Delhi, 1716
hookLine: hundreds of Sikhs are paraded and executed daily, and tradition says none renounced their faith

lines: A PROCESSION MEANT TO BE SEEN.
THE SAME WAY OUT, OFFERED TO EACH.
cards: A road from Punjab to the capital, and a procession on it that was meant to be seen. The captives from Gurdas Nangal, Banda Singh among them, were taken to Delhi and paraded through the streets in chains, before crowds.
The empire wanted everyone watching to understand what happened to people who rose against it. Then came the executions, a group at a time, day after day.
And tradition says every one of the captives was offered the same way out.

teach.h: GIVE UP YOUR FAITH, AND LIVE.
teach.b: The way out was simple. Give up your faith, and live. Tradition says the offer was made, and that not one of them took it.
That's the line: none renounced. Sikhs still tell one story from those days.

teach.h: A MOTHER PLEADS; HER SON REFUSES.
teach.b: A mother, tradition says, went to the officials and pleaded for her young son. He isn't really a Sikh, she told them; he was caught up with the others by mistake. And she was granted his release.
But when the order reached him, the young man refused it. He said, in the telling, that his mother was mistaken: he was a Sikh, and he would stay with his companions. And he died with them.
It's a hard story, and Sikhs don't tell it to make anyone want to die.

They tell it for what it shows about faith that's chosen, not inherited or assumed. He could have walked out, and nobody would have blamed him. He decided who he was out loud, at the worst possible moment.
There's a Sikh word for the whole of that life: sikhi.

teach.h: SIKHI KEPT TO THE LAST BREATH.
teach.b: The Ardas remembers those who kept their sikhi to their last breath, with their hair uncut, which for a Sikh is part of keeping faith whole.
The march to Delhi is part of that memory. Today asks nothing heroic of you.
But it leaves a quiet question behind: when it costs something small, a raised eyebrow, an awkward pause, do you say who you are, or let someone else say it for you?

how: Sikhs remember the captives taken to Delhi with Banda Singh Bahadur, of whom tradition says none gave up their faith, and the Ardas remembers those who kept their sikhi to their last breath.

o: the Sikh way of life, kept whole
a march to the capital in chains
the prayer said when gatherings close

games.q: you're a young captive. your mother has won your release by saying you aren't a Sikh. the order is in your hand. what do you do?
o: say you are a Sikh and stay with the others.
take it, and secretly keep your faith.
games.why: tradition says he told them his mother was mistaken, that he was a Sikh, and died with his companions.

practice: Sit upright, the way people stand when a name is read aloud, and hold in silence the people who were offered a way out and kept their faith instead; if faces come, let them be faces you'll never know.
When your mind wanders, return to the silence, as if you stood in a crowd that has gone quiet. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
